title: Separating the Density Wave Phase from Zero-Resistance Superconductivity in La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10}$
authors: P. Puphal, A. Suthar, B. Wehinger, V. Sundaramurthy, T. Priessnitz, M. Knauft, P. Sosa-Lizama, Y. -M. Wu, M. Hepting, J. Nuss, M. Isobe, P. A. van Aken, Y. E. Suyolcu, B. Keimer, H. Takagi, P. Reiss
abstract: Identifying the key ingredients for superconductivity under pressure in the Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates remains a formidable challenge, due to a complex interplay between structural variations, oxygen content and location, electronically ordered phases, and the need for high pressures to reach the superconducting phase. To disentangle these complex inter-dependencies, here we study a series of clean single crystals of trilayer La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10}$. We discover that enhanced biaxial, compressive pressures induce a zero-resistance state at a 60\% lower pressure compared to previous reports. At the same time, we completely separate the low-pressure density wave phase from superconductivity, effectively ruling out that soft, quantum critical fluctuations of the density wave order parameter act as the pairing glue in this system. Our results establish biaxial, in-plane pressures as a powerful tool for promoting superconductivity in nickelates, unifying the required pressure scales for superconductivity in different Ruddlesden-Popper structures, and providing a connection to the recently discovered thin film samples.
summary: This experimental study investigates the complex phase diagram of the nickelate $	ext{La}_4	ext{Ni}_3	ext{O}_{10}$ under high pressure. By applying controlled, anisotropic strain, the researchers successfully separated the density wave phase from superconductivity. They demonstrate that in-plane compression is a powerful tool, significantly lowering the pressure required to induce zero-resistance superconductivity.
main_problem: The central challenge is to identify the key physical ingredients governing superconductivity in Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates, specifically separating the influence of structural variations, oxygen content, and competing electronic orders like Density Waves (DW).
main_result: The study successfully separated the low-pressure DW phase from superconductivity and found that applying enhanced biaxial, in-plane compressive pressures significantly lowers the required pressure to achieve zero resistance by 60% compared to prior reports.
method: The research employed high-pressure electronic transport measurements (resistivity) using single crystals, complemented by high-pressure X-ray Diffraction (XRD) to track structural changes under different compression regimes.
model_or_system: The physical system is the trilayer nickelate $	ext{La}_4	ext{Ni}_3	ext{O}_{10}$, which is studied under extreme conditions using diamond anvil cells (DACs) to apply controlled, non-hydrostatic pressures.
key_observables: Zero-resistance state ($T_c^0$), Density Wave transition temperature ($T_{	ext{DW}}$), resistivity anisotropy ($ho_{zz}/ho_{ab}$), and lattice parameters.
important_parameters: Pressure (especially the difference between isotropic, out-of-plane, and enhanced in-plane compression), and temperature.
main_assumptions: The authors assume that the observed differences in superconducting pressure dependence are due to the specific type of applied stress (biaxial in-plane vs. out-of-plane).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagrams showing the separation of DW and superconducting regions under varying pressure environments, and show transport measurements ($R$ vs $T$ and $R$ vs $p$) for different compression types.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares transport measurements under different pressure environments (pseudo-hydrostatic, out-of-plane, in-plane) to disentangle the competing electronic orders (DW vs. SC) and establish the role of anisotropic strain.
why_interesting: This work directly probes the interplay between competing electronic orders (CDW/DW) and superconductivity in strongly correlated nickelates, a canonical problem in condensed matter physics relevant to high-Tc superconductivity.

These blocks are stacked vertically and are separated by a horizontal, in-plane shift, defining the rock salt layer at the interface. Our results reveal an outstanding crystallinity with long-range ordering of La4Ni3O10 trilayers only, without any evidence of stacking disorder or intergrowth of other Ruddlesden-Popper phases8–11. The overlay show the monoclinic unit cell featuring perovskite layers formed out of NiO6 octahedra and La layers, separated by rock salt layers. (b) In-plane and (c) out-of-plane electrical resistivities. The density wave transition temperature TDW is highlighted by a vertical dashed line. The inset to (c) shows the temperature dependence of the anisotropy ratio γ.

Figure 2. Density wave formation and superconductivity in La4Ni3O10 under different pressure environments. (a) Under (pseudo-) hydrostatic conditions, the density wave phase is suppressed at a rate of approximately −9 K/GPa. (b) Under dominant out-of-plane compression, the density wave phase is suppressed more slowly, which appears highly consistent with the existing literature. Incomplete superconductivity is observed above ≈15−20 GPa, and zero-resistance is observed above 40 GPa only. (c) In contrast, under enhanced in-plane compression, the density wave phase is suppressed much faster at a rate of approximately −18 K/GPa, and we observe a zero-resistance state above ≈17 GPa already.
